newsitem.title: UK: London gold seeks direction post Dutch bank sale.
newsitem.headline: London gold seeks direction post Dutch bank sale.

text.p: The gold market was confused and seeking direction at lower levels on Tuesday after it had had a night to ruminate on the sale of 300 tonnes of bullion announced by the Dutch central bank on Monday.
"But at least volatility is back which is great. It has brought people back in and re-created a two-sided market," one dealer added.
Gold fixed at $357.30 per ounce after $359.60 on Monday afternoon and a London close of $358.80/$359.30.
"The market is confused as to why it jumped after the sale announcement yesterday. Maybe it was too quick," a dealer said.
Gold gained about a dollar on Monday morning after the Dutch Central bank news which confirmed rumours of a sale from a central bank of around 10 million ounces (300 tonnes).
The rumours had been current in the market for weeks and were a key factor behind gold's loss of value late last year.
But any sense that the announcement lifted market fears about central bank gold being released dissipated overnight.
Asian business was dominated by selling from Switzerland partially on local client accounts and sales from Australia which overwhelmed steady physical buying, dealers said.
"There has been psychological damage because of the Dutch sale. The feeling is, "Which one is next?'" a dealer said.

Bullion analyst Andy Smith at Union Bank of Switzerland said, "Last week Gold Fields Minerals Servives said (net) 208 tonnes were sold (from the official sector) last year and the market thought that was too much. Now the Dutch have announced a 300-tonne sale and it doesn't think that's enough."
Short covering thwarted attempts in London to take the market lower. "We might try to going into Comex unchanged, but New York could take it lower again later," a dealer said.
In the near term gold looked likely to retest last week's lows when prices dipped below $354 an ounce, another said.
"The outlook doesn't look good. From a speculative point of view, the only reason to buy gold is if you think prices will go up. The central bank sales threaten the opposite," he said.
Longer term gold looked set to sink to the $350-$355 level.
There was no apparent impact from U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan warning central banks against being complacent in their continuing fight against inflation.
The other metals were quiet behind gold. Silver was two cents lower at $4.69/$4.71. Platinum ws down $0.75 at $361.75/$362.75 and palladium shed $1.10 to $121.00/$122.00.
